Let me check the latest.I couldn't check the Gaceta Oficial or the Metaculus FAQ directly. Everything below comes from news searches run on October 5, 2026. **As things stand, the question would resolve NO.** DS 5716 is in force and the government keeps saying it won't repeal it.

**Resolution sources**
- **Gaceta Oficial:** I couldn't load it, and none of my results mention any decree repealing or suspending DS 5716. A Bolivian legal blog posted the decree's text on Sept 19. It changes how diesel is priced and repeals one clause of an earlier decree, DS 5516 of January 13, 2026.
- **Metaculus FAQ:** Not fetched. As usual on Metaculus, "credible sources" means major news outlets.

**What the decree does**
- It was approved on Friday, Sept 18 and in force since Saturday 19 September. It raised diesel from Bs 9.80 to Bs 17.95 per liter (VAT included), about 83%.
- The price now tracks the cost of importing diesel. A reference price holds unless international prices move more than 5% either way. Diesel is also now a single price for everyone; large consumers no longer pay a separate rate.
- The government says the subsidy cost about $55 million a week and $2.7 billion a year.

**Government stance**
- **Sept 23:** Public Works Minister Zamora said "No hay vuelta atrás" ("there's no going back").
- **Sept 26:** Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco said "El decreto no se va a abrogar" ("the decree will not be repealed"). The government keeps offering talks.
- **Around Sept 28:** President Paz defended the cut and said international organizations had congratulated Bolivia.
- **Early October:** La Patria reports the government is holding firm on keeping the decree in force despite calls for dialogue.

**Pressure building**
- **Evo Morales's camp:** Morales called it a "criminal" decree. His supporters set an Oct 3 deadline to repeal DS 5716 and a second decree, 5727, and threatened a national mobilization starting October 13. That falls just before the resolution window.
- **Drivers' confederation:** Held a 24-hour strike on Sept 28, with uneven turnout. It went to talks in La Paz on Sept 29 and still demands repeal.
- **Santa Cruz transport:** Gave the government 48 hours and announced a strike on Monday Oct 5 and Tuesday Oct 6.
- **Mining cooperatives (Fencomin):** On about Sept 30 they decided to demand repeal of DS 5716. They also want the mining and hydrocarbons ministers to resign.

**Scheduled events before Oct 17**
- Oct 5–6: Santa Cruz transport strike.
- Oct 13: planned start of the Morales camp's national mobilization.
- Talks with transport groups are ongoing.

**Base rates and context**
- From what I remember (not confirmed in these searches), the same government repealed its December 2025 fuel decree, DS 5503, in January 2026 after protests led by the COB, Bolivia's main labor federation. It replaced it with DS 5516, which kept the fuel price increases. That shows a repeal-and-replace route exists.
- Under these rules, repealing DS 5716 and issuing a new decree with the same content would count as YES. Changing the price formula, cutting the price, or adding sector-specific relief while leaving DS 5716 in force would count as NO.
- Historically, fuel-price reversals in Bolivia have happened after protests escalated a lot. The best-known case is the "gasolinazo" of December 2010, when Morales withdrew a fuel price hike within about five days. Weeks of firm government statements, like these, usually suggest the policy stays.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find any market on this question.

**Resolution timing:** Only a repeal or suspension in effect at some point during Oct 15–17 counts. A repeal before Oct 15 would probably still be in effect then and count.

criterios: This question resolves YES if, at any time between October 15, 2026 and October 17, 2026 (inclusive), the government of Bolivia formally abrogates (repeals), derogates, or suspends the application of Supreme Decree 5716 of 18 September 2026 — the decree that eliminated the diesel subsidy and set the regulated diesel price at Bs 17.95 per liter. A formal repeal, derogation, or suspension is established by publication of a new Supreme Decree (or equivalent official norm) to that effect in the Gaceta Oficial del Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia (https://www.gacetaoficialdebolivia.gob.bo/), or by an official government announcement of such a measure reported by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions). It resolves NO if no such abrogation, derogation, or suspension has taken effect by the end of October 17, 2026 (Bolivia time, UTC−4).
letra_pequena: A measure that merely modifies the price-adjustment methodology, lowers the regulated price, adds compensatory social measures, or restores a partial subsidy for specific sectors — while leaving Supreme Decree 5716 formally in force — does not count. Only a formal repeal, derogation, or suspension of Supreme Decree 5716 as a legal norm triggers YES. A measure in force at any point during October 15–17, 2026 counts even if later reversed.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About 12 days, until the end of October 17 in Bolivia.

(b) **Status quo:** NO. Decree 5716 remains in force, and the government says it will not repeal it.

(c) **Reference class:** Contentious fuel-price reforms facing organized protests. As a rough judgment, not a measured statistic, I would put formal reversals within a month in the minority—perhaps 15–30%. Bolivia’s history of reversals raises the risk, while the IMF-linked financing and the government’s firm stance lower it.

(d) **NO scenario:** Protests begin on October 13, but the government holds its position, perhaps offering talks, price adjustments, or targeted relief without suspending or repealing the decree.

(e) **YES scenario:** Strikes and blockades rapidly become disruptive enough that the government formally suspends or repeals Decree 5716, possibly replacing it with another decree.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** A lower diesel price or partial subsidy alone does **not** count if Decree 5716 stays in force. Conversely, a formal repeal-and-replacement can count even if much of the policy survives. The qualifying measure must be in effect during October 15–17.

The short remaining window and the government’s continued refusal make NO substantially more likely, though the planned mobilization creates a real chance of a rapid reversal.

Probability: 22%

(c) **Reference class:** Bolivian fuel-price measures facing major protests. The 2010 reversal shows that rapid retreats happen, but it is only one close precedent. My rough, judgmental base rate for a *formal reversal within weeks* is **15–25%**, not a measured frequency.

(d) **NO scenario:** Protests intensify, but the government holds the decree in place while offering talks, compensation, or a lower price.

**(a) Time left:** 12 days, to the end of October 17, 2026 (Bolivia time). The resolution window itself is October 15–17.

**(b) Status quo:** NO. DS 5716 has been in force since September 19. Ministers and President Paz keep saying it will not be repealed ("no hay vuelta atrás"; "el decreto no se va a abrogar"). The IMF program, expected to be approved around October 2, depends on removing fuel subsidies.

**(c) Reference class:** Bolivian fuel-price hikes met by mass protest.
- In 2010 Morales reversed the gasolinazo within about five days.
- The most relevant precedent is this same government. It issued DS 5503 in December 2025, faced COB-led protests, and in January 2026 repealed it and replaced it with DS 5516, which kept the price increases. That took roughly 3–4 weeks of escalating pressure. My research assistant flagged this from memory and did not confirm it in the searches.

So repeal-and-replace is a proven tool for this administration. Across the reference class, reversal under sustained heavy protest happens perhaps 30–40% of the time. The chance that it lands in a specific three-day window, about 4 days after the main mobilization starts, is much lower.

**(d) NO scenario:** The Morales camp's mobilization starting October 13 is fragmented. The state of exception and the military restrict blockades. Transport unions settle for compensatory measures, such as targeted relief or tweaks to the price formula, while DS 5716 stays formally in force. The government holds firm through October 17, protecting the IMF deal.

**(e) YES scenario:** Protests escalate sharply from October 13. Mining cooperatives, transport unions and possibly the COB join the Morales camp, causing blockades and fuel or food shortages. By October 15–17 the government repeats its January playbook: it repeals DS 5716 and issues a new decree with similar or modified content, as a face-saving concession.

**(f) Technicalities:**
- A repeal-and-replace counts as YES even if the new decree keeps the Bs 17.95 price. That raises the odds relative to a "true reversal" question.
- Lowering the price or adding sector-specific subsidies while DS 5716 stays in force counts as NO.
- A repeal issued before October 15 would probably count, since it would still be in effect during the window.
- The Evo-led mobilization is politically weaker than the COB-led pressure that forced the January repeal. The government also has the state of exception and IMF backing.

Weighing the January precedent against the firm stance, the narrow timing and the weaker coalition, I put the probability around 12%.

Probability: 12%
